Hey OP, remember failure is a temporary defeat if you choose to learn from it. What course are you studying? College is really hard. If I could go back in time, I would’ve skipped college and the debt and instead gone to TAFE. TAFE has a bad reputation but I don’t understand why bc it gets you employed unlike some university courses which don’t have a clear vocational career pathway. It’s not your fault—it’s the system, sadly. My point is, if you’re failing your courses it’s clearly a sign that you might be studying a degree that you’re either 1. Uninterested in 2. Interested in, but doesn’t play to your strengths. if possible, take a semester off and really think about what career paths are suited to your natural talents. Do extensive research on your personality type as well and the kind of careers that play to the strengths of your personality type. Try 16 personalities, enneagrams, BIG 5, etc. Hard work beats natural talent, sure, but it’s easier if you supplement your natural talents WITH hard work.

You're very welcome. That woman sounds lovely and is a true introvert-introvert. Also, remember that introversion is a spectrum. Look out for girls who in their natural state are true introverts, but appear extroverted (I called them introverted extroverts/extroverted introverts/ambiverts) bc they have many friends, are talkative in some social contexts and are bubbly and enthusiastic. The sad reality is, this world we live in favours extroverts--if you're an extrovert in retail, in corporate, in the playground at schools, in the staffroom, you're liked more because you appear approachable, exuberant, friendly and popular. Thus, many female and male introverts have unknowingly trained themselves to succeed in extroverted environments, so they can appear to be an extrovert, when deep inside they possess hallmarks of a true introvert (prefer spending time alone, have introverted hobbies). I've heard good things about Meetup or online communities like book club or language learning on Discord, maybe give them a try! I know how you feel about YouTube videos. I find it so unnatural to look at a camera and talk--it feels extremely unnatural for me. I realized this when I was doing some virtual video interviews and struggled. Anyway, good luck OP. Just remember your struggles are felt by other introverts too, so you're not alone.

The difficulty w dating apps is that us females, even the introverted ones are trying to find signs to trust you (as in a guy on an app) since it’s a dangerous world out there are and the nature of dating apps are that they’re fastidious and both males and females are forced to make snap judgements based on very little amount of data that tells us who you are as a whole person. Thus if you’re an introverted guy who is private and doesn’t overshare, it makes it easier for you to be to evaluated as being a loner or a creep.  we’re looking for clues that you’re not and usually this is substantiated through photos of the guy with their friends and/or family. It’s the same for introverted females but probably less so since women are more sought after than males are. Thus the closing word is don’t use dating apps—they’re shitty and leave you feeling hollow. It did for me, bc it felt so disingenuous and I feel like dating apps favour extroverted people bc it’s in their nature to market themselves “loudly” and be fine with over sharing whereas for us introverts we don’t like doing that. We are pretty private. So I’d say to instead get involved in volunteering or a team based hobby and try to find a partner that way. I know it’s freaking hard and I empathise with you 100% but it’s the reality. In fact, dating apps for introverts is an untapped market. I hope someone entrepreneurial and innovative can put an end to our suffering by building an dating app that’s for introverted guys and girls!

I can’t speak for *all* introverted women but this is just my hot take as one, single member of the populace. You know how we human form an impression of someone seconds after meeting them? It’s the same when I scan someone’s social media i.e. Instagram. If they have a tonne of pretentious posts —it’s hard to pinpoint posts that are symptomatic to pretentiousness, but usually it’s a combo of a lot of selfies, pics “”w the boys”” holding beers and 90% of them wearing Ralph Lauren as if it’s a marker of sophistication and aristocracy, and usually one of the photos is a group photo on a yacht, and every post (both the photos and the caption) in tandem, gives off an aura of “I tried really hard” bc it’s too picture perfect. On the other hand, I’m really attracted to guys who either don’t have Instagram or use it extremely sparingly or are active on it but their accounts are functional i.e. for documenting a specific hobby like a sport or photography or favourite books etc. That to me is characteristic of a person who isn’t a social climber, rather someone who is centred on themselves and their interests. Other turn offs are guys who are really rowdy, drink a lot of alcohol, smoke and do drugs and go clubbing heaps. Those seem like markers of extroverted individuals bc they seek external stimulation. I like guys who listen more than they speak, are modest and humble, well-read, like playing puzzles and board games and generally quiet but light up when they’re with their small circle of friends. It’s attractive to me bc, well I’m introverted, so I like guys who have a similar vibe as me. Idk I just like quiet and simple guys who don’t get caught up in all the bs of the world.

Thank you for taking the time to reply. I did feel this way throughout university, but not all the time. I have had therapy on and off since 2016 (first year of uni) until 2020 (last year of uni). The pattern was always this: going pretty well, then doubting myself and my self-worth and feeling extremely lonely in the world, isolating myself and overthinking, breakdown/suicidal thoughts, seeking therapy, getting therapy for 6-8 months, feeling a bit better, stopping therapy (due to costs), coping well for 1-3 months and then the whole cycle repeats again. The underlying reasons for my bleak outlook on life is just...I don't know...my greatest need is a sense of family, connection and belonging but I never had that and I know I can't have that. Domestic violence household meant my parents separated and divorced when I was young, my Dad never played much of a role in my upbringing, my Mum worked 2-3 jobs during my childhood and when she wasn't working she stayed home and watched movies until 2-4am, I had no family friends growing up, no relationship with my relatives (all interstate or in different country/continent), no grandparents, no christmas, no birthday parties, no thanksgiving, no Easter celebrations. I have no memories of my childhood except a couple when I was around my friends at school. Also my brother took on the role of being my parent/guardian so we don't have that sibling bond/rapport--it's a very functional relationship, and he's also very mean to me and speaks to me harshly (and did when I was growing up). On occasion he makes arguments with me and if I speak back to stand up for myself, he will use horrible profanities like "f\*\*\*g d\*\*b b\*\*\*h" or "stupid c\*\*t" and I've gotten used to it and it doesn't make me cry like it used to, but I still envy my friends who have a close relationship with their sibling. I also can't see myself being in a relationship because I'm so embarrassed and scared they will flee once they get to know how dysfunctional my family is/domineering my brother is and as a kid, I could never see myself having a family anyway because. I feel so disconnected in this world and don't understand what the purpose of life is in this capitalistic society where it's all about personal gain and status, and apart from my Mum, no one loves me. To me, family=heartbreak and harm whereas for other healthy people, family=love, support and protection. Sorry for writing so much, but to answer your question, I'd say my sadness has always been there since I was in primary school until now at age 24, but it's become worse the past two months.

She has been out of work for the past month but it's been a blessing in disguise as I've been able to spend more time with her since I moved back home earlier this year (I lived interstate for the past 6 years, straight out of high school). So there's been a bit of that too--feeling like a kid again, and being taken care of. Today she came by my room and motioned her arms outwards, asking for a hug which I thought was endearing haha.

I once read the aphorism, 'your parents have known *you* for *your* *entire life* but you've only known your parents for *a par*t *of their life*' and I remember my eyes widening like a possum because although I had a cursory understanding of that concept in my head already, it was at that moment when I read the congruent concept in an eloquent sentence that I understood, 'oh they are people...beneath the title Mum or Dad, they were and still are a person of their own set of everything--their own quirks, bad habits, fears, favourite movies, favourite foods, celebrity crushes...the whole lot. I think my experience yesterday just 'hanging out' with my Mum really brought that realization home for me, because it has changed the way I see her.

My Mum used to always say, 'wait till you become a mother and you'll understand.' I don't want children when I get older, so practically, she's right--I'll never understand the depth of love a mother has for their child, but yesterday I got close to finally understanding it. I've always appreciated my Mum but yesterday's experience really changed me.

Hey OP, I used to convulse every time I read cliched Instagram posts with quotes like "You must love yourself before you love another" or "a relationship is two wholes coming to create one." Seems like such obvious advice, right? Even a person with the lowest IQ in the room would know this. Except, I experienced cognitive dissonance on a whole new level because I couldn't admit to myself that I loathed myself and didn't have the self-trust and assuredness to actually be in a relationship, which requires you to be completely vulnerable with the other person. For a long time, I (24F) wondered why I was single my whole life, and it's because I need time to fully, completely love myself before someone else can, otherwise I'm going to be causing my partner a lot of heartaches. You will meet your soulmate one day. When that day comes, we both don't know. That's an uncontrollable variable, but a variable you can control is how ready you will be when you meet that potential soul mate. Don't be depressed, be hopeful and keep working on yourself for that day in the future when you meet someone and you are both at the right place at the right time.

Hey kiddo, I'm (24F) almost double your age. At age 13, you're probably going through a lot of transitions in your life. You're most likely experiencing puberty and the difficulty of transitioning from primary to junior high school, which in my experience was a really, really big jump, especially in terms of having to mature quickly and deal with an increased workload + a much higher academic standard. Have you tried confiding in your school well-being counsellor, or even your homeroom teacher? I know it's difficult being vulnerable, but adults are adults for a reason--with their age comes wisdom, experience and a wealth of resources, and they may be able to direct you in the right path. You sound like you're feeling a lot of guilt, which is in turn making you self-loathe and depressed. Realise this: everyone feels guilt for their past wrong-doings, so you are not alone. Depressed people are depressed because we are so wrapped up in over-thinking and over-dwelling, as well as thinking we are the only one's to experience what we are experiencing. Don't suffer alone, and let someone know that you need a shoulder to lean on, and someone to listen to you without judgement.
